transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/time: 2025-02-27 16:00 UTC
- Duration: ~58 minutes
- Attendees: Jordan Kim (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Ethan Lowe (Redwood SE), Liam Ortiz (CTO, Cerulean), Sofia Wang (Lead Infra), Marcus Hale (SRE), Anika Rao (PM)

Summary (auto): Quick deep dive focusing on edge topology, multi-site VPC peering, KV cache hotspotting, and p95/p99 tail behavior for streaming vs non-streaming workloads. Agreed next steps: run targeted KV hotspot benchmark in staging, exchange topology diagrams, and follow-up pilot checklist for on-prem option.

Topics: edge proxies, multi-site VPC, p95/p99 tail, streaming fallbacks, non-streaming batching, KV cache hotkeys, quantization tradeoffs

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Jordan: ok hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll keep this focused — we have Priya and Ethan here from the infra side to run through the topology and perf details.
[00:12] Liam: yeah thanks Jordan, appreciate it. we're seeing intermittent p99 spikes with our assistant API, mostly during peak window 11am-1pm PST. p95 is fine but p99 jumps up to like 420-480 ms where baseline is ~120ms.
[00:28] Priya: got it. couple quick clarifying q's — is that measured at the edge gateway or after your internal proxy? are you doing streaming responses or single-shot non-streaming?
[00:40] Sofia: it's at the edge gateway, we have an nginx-layer edge proxy that terminates TLS then forwards to our VPC private subnet where the model endpoints run. currently we use streaming for conversational flows and non-stream for some batch inference.
[01:00] Ethan: perfect — that mixed mode often explains variance. streaming keeps sessions open and can amplify multi-hop jitter.
[01:12] Marcus: to add, we have two edge POPs in us-west1 and us-west2, traffic is routed by geoproximity. occasionally we see one pop overloaded and traffic flaps to the other, which coincides with p99 spikes.
[01:28] Priya: ok so potential multi-site handoff. are you using consistent KV cache replication or per-pop cold caches?
[01:36] Sofia: per-pop, we preferred local caches to reduce cross-pop latencies. but we suspect hotkeys are localizing and causing eviction storms.
[01:44] Jordan: eviction storms + streaming sessions + multi-hop proxying = classic tail pain. let's walk through the request path and the metrics you collect.
[01:56] Liam: sure. request path is: client -> edge POP (nginx) -> edge proxy -> VPC peering -> model fronting in cerulean-ml-subnet -> local kv cache (redis-like) -> model instance. sometimes we have an additional egress through a security appliance for inspection.
[02:20] Ethan: that additional hop (security appliance) can add 10-50ms variance especially under burst. also if proxy worker threads block on IO, streaming can pile up.
[02:36] Sofia: interesting, we do see thread utilization spikes on the edge during handoffs.
[02:44] Priya: a few axes to consider: 1) reduce multi-hop for tail SLOs (co-locate cache + model behind same pop), 2) use streaming timeouts and backpressure to avoid head-of-line blocking, 3) KV cache hotspot mitigation with sharding or local LRU adjustments, 4) quantization — smaller model runtimes reduce service time per token so p99 moves down.
[03:10] Marcus: on quantization, we've tried 4-bit (Q4) on smaller models but results were noisy, some regressions on rare prompting patterns — we can't sacrifice quality for the assistant flows.
[03:26] Jordan: that's expected; quantization reduces tail by reducing per-token compute but can increase variance for corner cases. we recommend A/B with eval prompt sets to guard quality.
[03:36] [03:36] Liam: can you explain how Redwood's streaming fallback works if the KV cache misses or if a model slower variant is required?
[03:46] Priya: sure — our runtime supports prefix caching and a streaming fallback: if a prefix fetch misses or the model is above a latency threshold, requests can be routed to a lighter quantized variant or to a cached completion. fallback routing is policy driven — latency-first vs cost-first. note: when we fallback to a quantized model we sometimes reduce max tokens to cut p99 tail.
[04:10] Ethan: important nuance — streaming keeps the connection open so fallback must coordinate with client restart semantics; if not, you get duplicate deliveries or truncation.
[04:22] Anika: that duplicate problem is exactly what we saw in last week's demo, yes.
[04:28] Priya: yeah, so we usually recommend an idempotent request id and a short stream-reconnect window so client resumes without double output.
[04:40] [04:40] Sofia: you mentioned KV sharding — how aggressive should we be? we've got a relatively small keyspace dominated by a small set of users.
[04:48] Priya: if you have hot keys concentrated, options are: local write-through caches per pop with asynchronous replication; client-side sticky routing so hot users hit the same model instance; or dynamic hotkey splitting (route top N keys to dedicated hot shards). each has tradeoffs in consistency and complexity.
[05:12] Marcus: dynamic hotkey splitting sounds heavy. we prefer stickiness first.
[05:18] Jordan: stickiness is low-friction. the downside is capacity unevenness — you'll need autoscaling policies that consider per-shard load rather than uniform CPU.
[05:28] Liam: let's talk numbers — with our baseline 120ms median, what p99 reductions should we expect with stickiness + co-locating cache?
[05:38] Priya: ballpark: stickiness + local cache can drop p99 by 30-40% for KV-related spikes. co-locating cache and model (same POP, same host rack) can shave an additional 10-20ms by removing the VPC hop. combine with batching changes and quantization you could see p99 approach ~150-200ms depending on prompt length.
[06:02] Ethan: caveat — batching reduces per-token cost but increases tail for single-request low-latency SLO; streaming tends to benefit from small, eager flushing.
[06:14] Sofia: hmm, we have mixed traffic — some low-latency assistant chats and some high-throughput embeddings.
[06:22] Priya: two advice lanes: carve separate endpoints (low-latency streaming path with small batch size, and throughput path with larger batch and q4 quantization). route by route policies are supported so clients pick appropriate endpoints.
[06:38] [06:38] Marcus: how does network jitter in VPC peering show up? we saw bursts that correlate with cross-region packet reordering.
[06:46] Ethan: packet reordering can delay TCP acking and cause retransmits — at application level that's seen as 50-200ms spikes. use GSO/TCP offload tuning and ensure MTU consistency across peering to reduce the effect. also enable keepalive probes so idle streaming sockets don't get NAT timeouts.
[07:06] Sofia: good, we'll check MTU and offload.
[07:12] Anika: any recommendations for instrumentation? we feel blind between edge and model.
[07:18] Priya: instrument at each hop: edge ingress, proxy handoff, vpc egress, cache lookup latency, model queueing time, and model decode latencies per token. Redwood ships tracing hooks with distributed trace IDs you can propagate. also create synthetic traffic that reproduces your peak distribution — keys, prompt lengths, and concurrency.
[07:44] Liam: synthetic traffic — can Redwood run that for us in staging? we don't want to perturb prod.
[07:50] Jordan: yes, Priya can run a controlled KV-hotspot benchmark in your staging with your topology. that's one of the next steps.
[07:58] [07:58] Sofia: when you run the benchmark, we'd like to see streaming vs non-streaming curves and percentile graphs.
[08:06] Priya: absolutely — we'll produce p50/p95/p99 charts, heatmaps for latencies over time, and breakdowns per hop. we'll also include tail correlation with CPU and network metrics.
[08:18] Marcus: what about batching config — you said batching can increase tails — how should we tune?
[08:24] Priya: for low-latency endpoints keep batch windows small (1-5ms) and max batch size small (2-8). for throughput endpoints allow bigger windows (10-50ms) and larger batch sizes. adaptive batching helps: if queue length exceeds thresholds, flush early. Redwood supports adaptive flush based on SLO policies.
[08:46] Ethan: also be careful with prefix caching. If you cache and then batch mismatched prefixes, you can end up with miss amplification — make sure cache keys include the prompt prefix fingerprint.
[08:58] Jordan: there's also cost tradeoff. smaller batches raise cost per token; there's a balance between cost and p99. we can run a cost-vs-latency sweep in the benchmark.
[09:10] Sofia: about on-prem — if we do private deployment in our DC, will that reduce p99 substantially?
[09:16] Priya: on-prem eliminates public VPC egress hops and cloud peering variance, so yes typically p99 tightens, but it introduces your network constraints. if your DC network is solid (good east-west bandwidth, low jitter) you'll see improvement. however, operational overhead and hardware sizing are non-trivial.
[09:34] Liam: understood. our preference is hybrid: edge in cloud POPs, model inference on-prem rack for sensitive data. can you support hybrid routing?
[09:44] Jordan: yes — policy based routing can route by tenant and by data residency tags. we can also pin certain users to on-prem slices.
[09:52] Anika: about quantization — you cautioned it's noisy on rare prompts. is there a middle ground?
[09:58] Priya: yes, mixed precision. use q8 for safety-critical routes and q4 for lower-risk endpoints. another pattern is output-level validation: run the generation on a fast quantized model, then spot-check on a higher-precision model for flagged patterns (e.g., hallucination risk).
[10:18] Marcus: that sounds compute heavy.
[10:20] Priya: it's heavier but you can sample, not every request. sample rate depends on risk tolerance.
[10:28] [10:28] Liam: let's walk through a hypothetical: user hits edge POP A, their hotkey isn't present so it goes to fallback across VPC to pop B and causes a cache fill; what's the typical latency penalty?
[10:40] Ethan: if cross-pop, add ~30-80ms network + runtime queuing. if security appliance in path maybe another 20-50ms. and if model needs warm KV load into memory, add model cold-load penalty which can be 100-300ms depending on model and caching strategy.
[10:58] Sofia: that aligns with our spikes, sometimes there's a 250ms bump.
[11:04] Priya: mitigation: pre-warm top keys in all pops or the proactive replication of top N keys during surge windows. pre-warming trades bandwidth for tail stability.
[11:18] Marcus: how do you detect surge windows reliably?
[11:22] Jordan: use rolling percentile monitors and burst detectors — Redwood can send alerts when p95 climbs 20% over baseline and trigger pre-warm workflows.
[11:34] Anika: ok — for the benchmark, can you simulate realistic user-key skew and session lengths?
[11:40] Priya: yes we'll parameterize: key skew (zipf alpha), session length distribution, token length distribution, and concurrency. we'll match to your historical metrics.
[11:52] [11:52] Sofia: any gotchas with TLS termination and keepalive interplay with streaming?
[11:58] Ethan: keepalive idle timeouts at edge and intermediate NATs can drop long-lived streaming sockets — use short application-level heartbeats or split the connection so that only the streaming portion remains alive. also ensure TLS session resumption is enabled to reduce handshake costs.
[12:18] Marcus: what about OS-level tuning? we've not touched NIC offloads or rscale.
[12:24] Priya: enable gro/gso/lro on NICs, tune net.core.rmem/wmem and TCP backlog, and ensure epoll/kqueue parameters suit high connection windows. these reduce syscall blocking and improve tail.
[12:38] Liam: great. can you also provide a checklist for pre-prod to prod migration so we don't accidentally create new tail sources?
[12:46] Jordan: yes we'll include a pre-prod checklist: tracing enabled, synthetic load test run, KV hotkey analysis, adaptive batching tuned, fallback policies defined, SLO alert thresholds configured.
[13:02] Anika: last question: are there known interactions between sharded KV and quantization that could increase tail?
[13:10] Priya: yes — if quantized model executes faster but cache fetch is still slow due to sharding mismatch you can actually expose the cache as the dominant tail. the fix is to rebalance cache latency to be below model execution median. in short: don't speed up compute without fixing data-plane.
[13:30] Sofia: makes sense.
[13:34] Jordan: ok let's recap next steps — Priya will run a targeted KV-hotspot benchmark in staging using your topology, Jordan will share quantization playbook and cost/latency sweep, Cerulean provides topology diagram and peak traffic profile, and we'll schedule the on-prem checklist follow-up week of Mar 3.
[13:56] Liam: thanks all. good session.
[14:00] End of recording.

Notes on transcription: occasional speaker overlap and some domain nouns may be mis-transcribed (e.g., model names). timestamps are approximate (every ~12-90 seconds) to reflect Fireflies export variety.
